name: Stoicism

card.summary: An ancient philosophy of virtue and control over judgments, now a popular self-improvement framework; no studies test it for looks.
card.note: Philosophy rather than a treatment; influence on cognitive therapy is historical.

quick.overview:
Stoicism is a school of philosophy founded in Athens around 300 BCE by Zeno of Citium. It teaches that virtue is the highest good and that distress comes from false judgments.

Today it is used as a practical self-discipline framework, including in self-improvement communities. No research evaluates Stoicism as an appearance intervention.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners focus on what is within their control and reframe judgments about events. Wikipedia notes this idea influenced rational emotive behaviour therapy and cognitive behavioural therapy.[1]
quick.risks: No physical risks. It is a philosophy, not a clinical treatment.

lead: Stoicism is a Hellenistic philosophy founded by Zeno of Citium in Athens around 300 BCE and developed by Chrysippus, and later Roman figures including Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius.[1] It holds that virtue is sufficient for a good life and that destructive passions arise from false judgments.[1]

In modern times it is presented as a practical guide to self-discipline, centred on distinguishing what is within one's control. Wikipedia notes that it inspired Albert Ellis's rational emotive behaviour therapy and shaped cognitive behavioural therapy.[1]
It is listed on the wiki as a mindset resource used in self-improvement culture. No studies connect it to appearance outcomes.

paras: The school took its name from the Stoa Poikile in Athens and was a leading philosophy of the educated Hellenistic and Roman world until about the 3rd century CE.[1] A neo-Stoic revival arose in the late 16th century, and scholars such as A. A. Long and Pierre Hadot renewed interest in the 20th century.[1]
Stoicism has linked parts of logic, physics and ethics. Health, wealth and pleasure are treated as indifferent, with value only as material for virtue.[1]

No studies found of Stoicism as an appearance or looksmaxxing intervention. Its historical influence on cognitive therapies is noted by Wikipedia, but that is distinct from testing Stoic practice itself.[1]

timeline.event: Zeno of Citium founds the school in Athens.[1]
A. A. Long's Problems in Stoicism is often cited as the start of the 20th-century scholarly revival.[1]
